title: /65e2d93b-6fb9-4809-b513-82332caa85c4/t1
text:
**Short answer:** small models are very cheap per token, but a VM you run yourself is usually *not* cheaper than a hosted API until you keep a GPU busy. The figures below are from memory and approximate, so check live prices before committing.

## Rough numbers

| Option | Cost | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| DeepSeek API | ~$0.30 in / ~$0.50–1.10 out per M tokens | Cache hits are roughly 4x cheaper. Already very cheap. |
| Hosted open small models (Together, DeepInfra, Fireworks, OpenRouter, Groq) | ~$0.02–0.15 per M tokens for 2B–14B | Pay per token, nothing to run, scales to zero. |
| Rented GPU (4090 or L4 on RunPod/Vast/GCP) | ~$0.35–0.80/hr, about $250–600/mo always-on | One card serves a 2B–9B model to many concurrent users. |
| CPU-only VM running gemma2:2b | ~$30–60/mo | About 10–20 tok/s per stream. Fine for a demo, not for scale. |
| H100 | ~$2–3/hr | Overkill for 2B–14B. |

## The catch is utilization

A 9B model on one 4090 or L4 with vLLM can push about 1–3k tokens/s aggregate when batched. A 2B model gets several times that.

- At full load, 1.5k tok/s on a $0.50/hr card works out to about **$0.09 per M tokens**. That's competitive with the hosted APIs.
- At 10% load it's about **$0.90 per M tokens**, which is worse than the API. You pay for the card whether or not anyone is asking.

Self-hosting wins when you have steady, high traffic. It loses when traffic is bursty or low. The rough break-even is 40–50% sustained utilization.

## Best way at scale, in order

1. **Hosted open-model API first.** Gemma and Qwen are already on the providers above. It's an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so moving to or from it is a base-URL change. Start here until your monthly bill is large enough to matter.
2. **Serverless GPU** (Modal, RunPod Serverless, Baseten) once you want your own weights or fine-tunes. You pay per second and it scales to zero. The cost is 10–30s cold starts.
3. **Dedicated vLLM or SGLang on reserved or spot GPUs**, behind a router with autoscaling, once load is steady. These make it cheap:
   - **Continuous batching**, which vLLM does by default.
   - **Prefix caching.** Your system prompts and grammars repeat, so this is nearly free savings.
   - **AWQ or FP8 quantization**, which fits more concurrent users per card.
   - **Escalation:** the small model answers by default and only hard cases go to a bigger model or DeepSeek.

## What this means for the-fold

Your design is the case where this works out best. The fold does the reasoning and the model only fills small slots. That means short outputs, repeated prompts, and 2B–14B models. One L4-class card could serve a lot of users. In the best case it isn't a GPU bill at all: the Heimdall/WebLLM path runs the model on each visitor's own browser GPU. Inference then costs you nothing, and it scales with users instead of with your spend.

**My recommendation:**
- Keep WebLLM as the default, as you already have it.
- Put a hosted small-model API behind it as the fallback for devices that can't run it.
- Only rent a dedicated GPU if the fallback traffic turns out to be both large and steady.

I can sketch the router layer in the fold (WebLLM, then hosted, then DeepSeek escalation) if you want. If you'd rather have current prices than my approximations, I can pull them live.

title: /65e2d93b-6fb9-4809-b513-82332caa85c4/t2
text:
That tracks with how the fold is built. Your product rules (find, snip and cite without rewriting, and the model never authoring the final words) move the hard part out of the model and into the pipeline. The runtime model ends up doing slot-filling and routing, and a 2B–14B model can do that.

A frontier model can still earn a place in three spots:

- **Building the thing.** Writing and refactoring code across this repo, as in this session, is where small local models are still clearly behind. That's a dev-time cost, not a per-user one.
- **Judging.** A stronger model as a falsifier or grader for your evals is cheap, because it only runs offline on a fixed set of asks.
- **The long tail at runtime.** Messy or ambiguous questions, rare languages, and long multi-document synthesis, where the structure you've built doesn't give the model a scaffold. This is the only runtime reason, and it should be a small fraction of traffic.

You can measure this instead of guessing. Run your existing ask set (`eval/snips/asks.json`, the Popper driver) through the small model and through one frontier model, and diff the failures. Every ask where the frontier model wins is a concrete remaining reason. Each one then either becomes a pipeline fix (more structure, so the small model stops needing help) or goes on an explicit escalation list. If the list stays short, you have your answer in data. In production you can keep a counter on how often escalation fires, so the number of reasons is tracked instead of felt.

I can wire that A/B into the falsifier driver if you want it. It would be one flag to swap the answer model and a report of which asks flip.

title: /65e2d93b-6fb9-4809-b513-82332caa85c4/t3
text:
Here are my picks, grouped by how much operating work you want to take on. Providers add and drop models often (older Gemma 2 listings especially), so check the current catalog before you commit.

## 1. Hosted per-token (no servers to run, scales to zero)
- **OpenRouter** is a router over many providers, with some free models. It fits your free-bench idea and gives you fallback across providers for free.
- **Together, Fireworks, DeepInfra** are the cheapest and most reliable for Gemma and Qwen at 2B–14B. All are OpenAI-compatible.
- **Groq** is extremely fast, but the model list is narrow.
- **Cloudflare Workers AI** runs at the edge, is cheap, and has a small model catalog. It's a good fit if the fold's server already sits near Cloudflare.

## 2. Serverless GPU (your own weights, pay per second)
- **Modal** has the best developer experience, scales to zero, and cold starts are tolerable. It's my top pick if you want to run your own vLLM.
- **Google Cloud Run with L4 GPUs** is serverless and scales to zero. You deploy a vLLM or Ollama container like any other service.
- **RunPod Serverless, Baseten** are the alternatives. RunPod is cheaper, and Baseten is more production-polished.

## 3. Dedicated GPUs (once load is steady and utilization is high)
- **Hetzner dedicated GPU boxes** are the cheapest always-on option, at a fixed monthly price per card.
- **Lambda, CoreWeave, RunPod pods** all work for reserved capacity.
- **Vast.ai** is the cheapest but varies in reliability. Use it for batch and eval work, not user-facing traffic.
- **AWS g6 or GCP L4 on Kubernetes** with autoscaling is the heavyweight route. Only worth it if you already live in that cloud.

## The engine on whichever box
Run **vLLM** (or **SGLang**) for batching and prefix caching, behind an OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Don't use Ollama for real traffic. It's fine for your Mac and for development, but it doesn't batch well.

## Putting it together for the fold
1. Keep **WebLLM** as the default, so there's no server cost.
2. Put **OpenRouter** or **Together** behind it as the fallback. This is one base-URL config and needs no new infrastructure.
3. When the fallback traffic becomes large and steady, move that load to **Modal or Cloud Run GPU** running vLLM. Still no always-on GPU bill.
4. Only buy a **Hetzner or Lambda** card when you can show high sustained utilization.

Put a thin router in front of all of it (**LiteLLM** or a few lines in the fold). Then every tier looks identical to the app, and you can swap providers by changing a config entry instead of rewriting code.

text:
I looked at the heimdall code. There are two separate places things queue, and they need different fixes.

## Browser tier (WebLLM): don't try to fix batching here
`WorkerEngine` in `heimdall/src/llm.js` chains jobs on one promise, so each engine runs one job at a time (the file's own comment says "one model serves one job at a time"). It already reports `pending` as backpressure to other heimdalls. A single user's WebGPU can't usefully batch anyway, so the scaling answer here is more peers, which is the design you already have. Swapping the engine (wllama, transformers.js) wouldn't help, because none of them batch either.

## Server floor: this is the actual bottleneck
The floor is Ollama behind khora's channel proxy on 11434, which `floor.js` notes "queues one request at a time and can refuse". That's the serial queue you'd feel at scale. Candidates for replacing it:

| Swap | Where it fits | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **vLLM** (or SGLang) | NVIDIA box | Continuous batching, prefix caching, and the best throughput by a wide margin. This is the real answer for hosting. |
| **llama.cpp `llama-server`** | Your Mac or a CPU box | Continuous batching via `--parallel N`, OpenAI-compatible, Metal support. As far as I know, recent versions enable continuous batching by default, but verify. |
| **MLX server** | Apple Silicon | Faster than llama.cpp on a Mac, with weaker batching. |
| **Ollama with `OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL`** | Zero-code stopgap | Gets you some concurrency, but it's weaker than the others. |

## How they plug in
- **Native link, no code change.** `runOnLink` in `bridge-server.mjs` already speaks an `openai` link kind (`/v1/chat/completions` with SSE). vLLM or llama-server can be registered as a native link today.
- **As the floor, needs a shim.** The floor path forwards Ollama's wire (`/api/chat`, `/api/generate`, `/api/tags`, `/api/version`), and vLLM only speaks `/v1/*`. You'd add a small `/api/chat` to `/v1/chat/completions` translation. There's already precedent for the reverse direction in the `/v1/messages` translator around line 979.
- **Routing model.** `executors.js` estimates latency as `queue × service-time`, which assumes a serial backend. A batched backend should report concurrent slots instead. Otherwise the router will wrongly steer traffic away from it under load.

## Recommendation
1. Don't touch WebLLM.
2. Bypass khora's single queue by pointing the floor at a batching server directly.
3. Start with llama-server on the Mac, since vLLM needs an NVIDIA card. Move to vLLM on a rented GPU once you want real scale.
4. Turn on prefix caching, since your system prompts repeat heavily.

Want me to wire the vLLM or llama-server link into heimdall and write the Ollama-wire shim? Heimdall has uncommitted edits from other sessions, so I'd confirm with you before editing it.

text:
The first slice works. You can paste a key for OpenRouter, Together, Fireworks or DeepInfra in Settings, and the Fold can send one request to several of their small models at once. The Matrix part and the batching changes are not built yet. Nothing is committed.

Heimdall's tests pass (517) and the Fold's pass (1320). I also checked the Settings panel in a browser. I haven't run any of this against a real provider, because I can't enter keys. The tests use stubbed providers and fake keys.

## Built
- **Key rows:** Settings now has OpenRouter, Together, Fireworks and DeepInfra rows next to Anthropic and OpenAI. Saving a key tests it live, then registers up to three small models (Gemma, Qwen or Llama, 14B or under, no reasoning models) that the key's own model list confirms. It never registers the full catalogue.
- **Parallel calls:** a new `POST /api/race` in heimdall, with `race()` in the Fold's client. By default it picks one model per provider, so the lanes really differ. `mode: "first"` returns the first success, and `"all"` waits for every lane so you can compare or witness. It uses the same sealed privacy gate as chat, and each lane uses its own key.
- **Cost tier:** these models are now counted as cheap "open remote", not frontier, in dispatch, the ledger and the Fold's tier list.

## A bug I found and fixed
URLs for providers whose base ends in `/v1` (OpenRouter, Groq and others) were built as `.../v1/v1/chat/completions`. That returns a 404, which the key probe counts as reachable, so these lanes would have looked live and never answered. An old discovery test had mocked the doubled URL, which is why it never caught this. I fixed the URL building and corrected that test.

## Not done yet
- **Matrix and "our own servers":** only a small function exists (`hostedHello`) that describes the hosted lanes in the peer layer's own format, with no key in it. Making them real fleet members depends on the peers and headless-controller work your notes say isn't wired into any server yet.
- **Batching:** the router still assumes serial backends. A concurrency-slots field in `executors.js`, a vLLM or llama-server link, and the Ollama-wire shim for the floor are all still to do.
- **Race cost:** in `first` mode the slower calls keep running and still bill, because there is no cancel yet. Small models make that cheap, but it's real.
- **Default model ids:** they are my best guesses and get checked against the key's own list. If an id has moved, the key falls back to the best small models in that list.

Next I'd do the concurrency slots and the vLLM/llama-server link, since both are small. The Matrix presence needs the peer wiring first, so I'd want your go-ahead before touching that. Heimdall has other sessions' uncommitted work, so I haven't committed anything.

text:
The settings changes are in. The demo and the tests were all run with fake keys against a stand-in provider, and nothing has been tried with a real provider yet. I stopped the demo server and deleted its temp folders. Fold tests are 1330/1330 and heimdall's are 518/518.

**Where the keys came from.** I made them up: placeholder strings like `sk-or-DEMO-FAKE-0011`, which I typed in myself. They only went to a stand-in provider I wrote that accepts any non-empty key, so no real provider was contacted. I checked that none ever reached your real `~/.heimdall`, and the temp copies are gone. You still need to paste your own keys.

**Easier to read.**
- **Key result:** it now shows a one-line headline, what the key unlocked, and a "+ Details" fold for the rest.
- **Settings modal layout:** every section collapses, and **API keys** is last. General is open by default and the rest start closed. Each section remembers whether you left it open.
- **Look:** no pills or boxes, just hairline dividers.

**Clickable account setup.** Each key row has **Get a key ↗**, which opens that provider's key page in a new tab. I checked the addresses resolve:
- Anthropic
- OpenAI (blocks my check but is the well-known address)
- OpenRouter
- Together
- Fireworks (the address I first tried returned a 404, so I used a different one)

- **Slots:** the router's wait estimate assumed one request at a time. It now counts "slots", the number of requests a backend takes at once, and with one slot it behaves exactly as before. - **Race:** the parallel race skips a lane that is full. If every lane is full, the least loaded one still takes the call.
